titre: A Court Older Than the Law Said to Have Founded It
accroche: In 1641, the English Parliament abolishes a court by claiming that a 1487 statute created it. Historians today think that is not true.
contenu_vulgarise:
In June 1637, William Prynne appears before a court with no jurors. A former lawyer, he has published a pamphlet judged seditious; the sentence falls the same day: the pillory, both ears cut off, both cheeks branded with the letters “SL” for seditious libel. No appeal is possible. The court that has just tried him sits in a room at Westminster whose ceiling is dotted with painted stars, hence its name: the Star Chamber.

## A Birth Nobody Can Date

The story usually told is that Henry VII created it by a statute of 1487, known as *pro camera stellata*, to try men too powerful for twelve local jurors to dare convict. It is, in fact, the story that the Parliament that abolished it in 1641 chose to adopt itself. But that same starred room had housed the king's council sitting as a court since the late 14th century at least, well before Henry VII: the room itself was built as early as 1347. “The court did not owe its existence to a statute of 1487,” sums up Encyclopedia.com, even if some later commentators believed it was its origin. The parliamentarians of 1641 were already debating the question: according to the historian Krista Kesselring, a specialist of the period, they wondered whether the court had been created by that statute, which it had manifestly exceeded, or whether it had an older history that might explain some of its excesses.

The court in fact grew by sedimentation: an informal royal council, without a jury, able to summon, question and decide quickly, which over the centuries handled what the ordinary courts could not try, notably because local jurors feared reprisals from an overly influential defendant.

## A Convenient Story

In 1641, the Long Parliament wants to abolish the court, but it needs a solid legal ground. Two options present themselves: either the court draws its power from an ancient royal prerogative, and confronting it means challenging the king's very authority over justice, a slippery terrain in the midst of a crisis with Charles I; or it draws its power from an ordinary statute, which Parliament can then repeal by an equally ordinary statute. The Commons debate, and in May choose the second version. The act passed on July 5 reproaches the court with having exercised “an arbitrary power,” which had become “an intolerable burden to the subjects,” and abolishes it by presenting it as the creation of a text of 1487 that, according to the act, it had betrayed.

The court had nonetheless well earned its end: during Charles I's personal rule, with no Parliament to oppose it, it became the instrument of power against its critics, Prynne being just one example among many. But the ground adopted for abolishing it (the betrayal of a mandate from 1487) is a convenient simplification, not a historical discovery.

## What the Expression Kept

Everyday English still says “star chamber” for a judgment rendered without adversarial hearing or recourse: a disciplinary committee, a closed administrative procedure. The expression has outlived the institution by almost four centuries. What it lost along the way is the doubt about its origins: we remember the legend that the Parliament of 1641 chose for the convenience of its own vote, not the older and more uncertain history that historians reconstruct today.

carte.punch: The Parliament that abolished the Star Chamber in 1641 invented its birth in 1487.
carte.idee: The Star Chamber had sat without a jury since the late 14th century. In 1641, Parliament abolishes it by claiming that a 1487 statute had created it, a story more convenient than true: the court is older, born of a royal council, not of a text of law.

quiz.question: Why does the Parliament of 1641 choose to say the Star Chamber was created by a statute of 1487?
choix: Because archives had just been found proving that date conclusively and definitively
Because King Charles I himself had proposed this version of its origin to the assembled Commons
Because a court born of a statute could be abolished by a statute, without challenging the king's authority
Because the 1487 statute had explicitly provided for its own repeal by Parliament
quiz.explication: The court could just as well have drawn its power from an ancient royal prerogative, perilous constitutional ground in the midst of the crisis with Charles I. Tying it to a statute of 1487 allowed it to be abolished by an equally ordinary statute, without opening that larger debate.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the sentence passed on William Prynne in June 1637 reveal about how the Star Chamber worked?
choix: It proves an accused could obtain a dismissal after a jury's deliberation
It proves the case was sent back to a common-law court on appeal
It shows a court without a jury, passing sentence the same day with no appeal possible
It shows the court limited itself to handing down merely symbolic fines
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Prynne appears before a court with no jurors; the sentence, pillory, cropped ears, branded cheeks, falls the same day, and no appeal is possible.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does Encyclopedia.com say about the real origin of the Star Chamber, compared with the story of a 1487 creation?
choix: That recently found archives confirm the 1487 date beyond doubt
That the court did not owe its existence to a statute of 1487, the room having been built as early as 1347
That the court only began to operate in 1603, under James I
That the 1487 statute really is the source of the court, applied a century later
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Encyclopedia.com states explicitly that the court did not owe its existence to a statute of 1487, the room having been built as early as 1347 and the royal council sitting there well before Henry VII.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What has survived of the Star Chamber in everyday English, almost four centuries after its abolition?
choix: A legal precedent still cited before British courts
The room itself, still used as a court at Westminster
A specific criminal offense that still bears the court's name
The expression “star chamber,” for a judgment rendered without adversarial hearing or recourse
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Everyday English still says “star chamber” for a closed procedure, without adversarial hearing or recourse, like a disciplinary committee.
